harder.verification_criterion: The answer explains at least one specific mechanism by which magnesium directly affects potassium regulation in the body (such as magnesium's role in Na-K-ATPase pump function or renal potassium handling).

attempts.answer:
Below is an evidence‑based map of how sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), magnesium (Mg2+), and calcium (Ca2+) relate to each other and to “other” ions in the body. I group mechanisms into (1) distribution and gradients, (2) transporters and channels that couple ions across membranes, (3) hormonal and renal regulation, (4) functional physiology (nerve/muscle/excitability), and (5) inter‑ionic interactions and clinical cross‑talk. Where relevant, I note “other” ions such as chloride (Cl−), bicarbonate (HCO3−), phosphate (HPO4^2−), hydrogen (H+), and water.

1) Where the ions live: gradients and the pumps that create them
- Na+ is predominantly extracellular and K+ predominantly intracellular, with Na+/K+-ATPase actively maintaining ~30:1 K+ inside versus outside the cell and ~5–10 mM intracellular Na+ despite continuous leakage; this gradient is the energy-dependent basis for resting membrane potential and action potentials in neurons and muscle. <cite id="c5ddf2a5-0">Na/K-ATPase is an integral membrane protein responsible for the transport of sodium and potassium across the plasma membrane in an ATP-dependent manner, composed of α and β subunits with tissue-specific isoforms; aldosterone and glucocorticoids regulate α and β subunit expression in a tissue-specific way</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-1">Na+-K'-ATPase pumps in the membrane maintain the low sodium, high potassium content of the cell; in collecting duct, aldosterone rapidly increases Na entry via apical channels coupled to Na'-K'-ATPase–dependent basolateral Na extrusion, with recruitment of latent pumps under Na load and aldosterone</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-2">In cortical collecting duct, aldosterone increases Na-K-ATPase number/activity and Na entry; interestingly, Na-K-ATPase can also be induced in some disease states (e.g., nephrosis) with sodium retention despite reduced ENaC, and in other models, aldosterone-independent regulation and local MR signaling can alter Na-K-ATPase with associated serum K changes</cite>.
- Mg2+ is mostly intracellular and is an essential cofactor of Na+/K+-ATPase and many enzymes; its availability also modulates excitability via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and NMDA receptors. <cite id="81319e7a-0">Magnesium serves as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes and is essential for maintenance of electrical potential of membranes; the Na/K pump is activated by magnesium, with ATP supplied as the Mg-ATP complex; magnesium deficiency impairs pump activity and K gradient maintenance</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-1">Magnesium homeostasis is intricately intertwined with K+, Na+, and Ca2+ via Na+/K+-ATPase, Ca2+-activated K+ channels, and other regulatory pathways, with roles in neural conduction and control of neuronal excitability</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is a divalent cation absorbed in intestine and excreted by kidney; it is a cofactor for Na+/K+-ATPase, protein kinases, and cyclase; as a calcium channel antagonist, Mg blocks NMDA receptors in a voltage-dependent manner and is required for vitamin D activation</cite>.
- Ca2+ has a low extracellular concentration but high intracellular sequestration in ER/SR; plasma membrane Ca2+ transport couples to Na+ gradients and hormonal control. <cite id="1215616c-0">In thick ascending limb, NKCC2 and ROMK facilitate reabsorption of cations (Ca2+ and Mg2+) via paracellular pathways (claudins 10/14/16/19); activation of the Ca-sensing receptor by high Ca inhibits NKCC2 via effects on ROMK and suppresses paracellular Ca absorption</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">In the loop of Henle, NKCC2/ROMK/Na+/K+-ATPase create a lumen-positive gradient that drives Ca and Mg reabsorption through paracellular movement; CaSR modulates Na+/K+-ATPase and NKCC2; in DCT, Mg reabsorption uses TRPM6/TRPM7 on the luminal side and SLC41A1 basolaterally, with Na/K ATPase and Na/Mg counter-transport shaping Mg handling</cite>.

2) Transporter and channel couplings that make “how they affect each other” concrete
- Na+/K+-ATPase is the fundamental bidirectional hub: it extrudes Na+ and imports K+ using ATP-Mg, and its abundance/activity is tuned by aldosterone and glucocorticoids, with isoform specificity across tissues. <cite id="c5ddf2a5-0">Na/K-ATPase α1/β1 are widely expressed; α2 predominates in skeletal muscle; α3 in excitable tissues; aldosterone and glucocorticoids regulate α and β subunit expression in a tissue-specific manner via MR and GR binding to promoter sequences</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-1">Aldosterone increases apical Na entry and Na-K-ATPase–dependent basolateral Na extrusion in CCD; Na+ itself can recruit latent pumps to the membrane, aldosterone-dependent</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-0">ATP-Mg2+ is the energy substrate for Na/K pump; Mg deficiency reduces pump energy and K gradient, increasing membrane permeability</cite>.
- DCT/CCD “aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron” switches Na, K, and Mg fluxes: ENaC on apical side mediates electrogenic Na reabsorption; ROMK and big-K (BK) channels secrete K; NCC in DCT1 provides electroneutral Na reabsorption. These operate as a unit to tune urine Na/K. <cite id="1215616c-2">In the ASDN (DCT2, CNT, CCD), ENaC orchestrates predominant electrogenic Na+ reabsorption, generating a lumen-negative transepithelial voltage that drives potassium secretion via ROMK and BK channels; DCT1 uses NCC for electroneutral Na reabsorption; DCT2 co-expresses NCC and ENaC with ROMK, enabling switching between electroneutral and electrogenic Na handling to adjust urinary K and Na to diet</cite>.
- Mg in the loop and distal nephron: paracellular shunting in thick ascending limb and specific reabsorption in distal convoluted tubule and CCD via TRPM6/TRPM7 and basolateral SLC41A1 with Na/K-ATPase; coupled to Cl− and Na+ transporters and CaSR feedback. <cite id="1215616c-0">In thick ascending limb, NKCC2 and ROMK create an electrochemical gradient that drives Ca2+ and Mg2+ reabsorption through tight junctions (claudins 10/14/16/19); CaSR activation by high Ca inhibits NKCC2 via ROMK and suppresses paracellular Ca/Mg movement</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">Loop of Henle: lumen-positive gradient formed by NKCC2/ROMK/Na+/K+-ATPase promotes Ca/Mg paracellular reabsorption; distal convoluted tubule Mg reabsorption occurs through TRPM6/TRPM7 (luminal) and SLC41A1 (basolateral), which acts as a Na/Mg counter-transporter; flow-dependent K secretion (BK), NCC on apical side, and voltage-gated Cl channels modulate Mg flow</cite>.
- Cross-talk among Na, K, Ca, and Mg at the cell membrane and synapse: 
  • Na/K pump sets the resting potential; voltage-gated Na channels open briefly, depolarize; delayed K efflux via KCa/ROMK and Na/K pump restores repolarization; Ca2+ enters through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels during the action potential, and Mg2+ is a physiological blocker of NMDA channels, limiting Ca entry and excitotoxicity. <cite id="81319e7a-1">Homeostasis among K, Na, Ca is maintained via Na+/K+-ATPase and Ca2+-activated K+ channels, fundamental to neural conduction and neuronal function</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium blocks NMDA receptors in a voltage-dependent manner, acting as a calcium channel antagonist and stabilizing excitability</cite>.
  • In muscle contraction, Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum lowers troponin affinity for actin; Mg2+ supports ATP-dependent Ca extrusion (SERCA-like) indirectly via ATP availability and Ca-channel modulation; K efflux through slow channels and Na/K pump hyperpolarizes to stop contraction. <cite id="81319e7a-0">Magnesium supports energy metabolism and membrane electrical potential in muscle and nervous tissue</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is required for ATP-dependent processes including neuromuscular conduction and antioxidant glutathione synthesis</cite>.

3) Hormonal and renal orchestration: the “orchestra conductor” that links the ions
- Mineraloccorticoids (aldosterone) and glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol) upregulate Na+/K+-ATPase and coordinate apical Na entry and basolateral Na extrusion; they also tune K secretion and Na reabsorption in distal nephron. <cite id="c5ddf2a5-0">Aldosterone and glucocorticoid hormones regulate α and β subunits of Na/K-ATPase with tissue specificity; MR and GR bind promoter DNA to enhance gene expression</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-1">Aldosterone increases Na entry via apical channels and Na-K-ATPase–dependent Na extrusion in CCD, with Na+ load recruiting latent pumps in an aldosterone-dependent manner</cite> <cite id="1215616c-2">ASDN integrates ENaC- and NCC-driven Na transport with ROMK/BK K secretion to adjust Na/K output with aldosterone-sensitive control</cite>.
- Calcium sensing and cross-talk: the Ca2+-sensing receptor (CaSR) in distal nephron links Ca2+ to NKCC2/ROMK and Na+/K+-ATPase, suppressing Na and Mg reabsorption when Ca is high, thus coordinating Ca, Na, and Mg handling. <cite id="1215616c-0">Activation of CaSR by high Ca levels inhibits NKCC2 via effects on ROMK and suppresses paracellular Ca absorption through claudin modulation</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">CaSR on loop of Henle cells influences Na+/K+-ATPase and NKCC2, which inhibits their activity and controls the electrochemical gradient that drives Ca and Mg reabsorption</cite>.
- Magnesium’s systemic endocrine links: Mg is a cofactor for vitamin D activation to 1,25(OH)2D and for kinases; Mg deficiency undermines energy supply to Na/K pump and can impair insulin’s effects, with clinical reviews detailing causes and treatments of hypomagnesemia and hypermagnesemia. <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is a cofactor for Na+/K+-ATPase and protein kinases and is required for conversion of vitamin D into 1,25(OH)2D</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-0">With magnesium deficiency, ATP-Mg complex is insufficient for the Na/K pump, impairing K influx into cells and compromising the membrane barrier</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">Renal Mg reabsorption involves TRPM6/TRPM7 and SLC41A1 and is modulated by distal transporters (NCC, ENaC) and channels (ROMK, BK), providing a nephron-wide link between Na, K, and Mg handling</cite>.
- Dietary and lifestyle levers: potassium-rich and low-salt diets lower BP by shifting distal nephron handling from NCC to ENaC dominance, increasing K loss and reducing Na retention; this reconfiguration illustrates Na↔K↔Mg coupling across the collecting duct. <cite id="1215616c-2">Potassium intake lowers blood pressure, with the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron switching between NCC (electroneutral Na reabs) and ENaC (electrogenic Na reabs) to adjust urinary K and Na; ENaC-driven reabs generates a lumen-negative voltage that drives K secretion via ROMK and BK channels</cite>.

4) Functional physiology: nerve, muscle, heart, and ECG-level consequences
- Resting membrane potential and excitability: Na/K pump establishes the K gradient that drives K efflux during hyperpolarization and sets the threshold; Ca2+ entry during depolarization is limited by Mg2+ block at NMDA receptors, limiting neuronal excitation and preventing arrhythmias. <cite id="81319e7a-1">Na+/K+-ATPase and Ca2+-activated K+ channels maintain ion homeostasis that underpins neural conduction and neuronal function</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium blocks NMDA receptors, controlling neuronal excitability and acting as a physiological calcium channel blocker</cite>.
- Neuromuscular contraction and arrhythmia risk: Mg2+ supports ATP supply and blocks Ca2+ entry; K+ efflux via channels/pump terminates action potentials and repolarizes; Na+ influx initiates depolarization. Imbalances create risk profiles: hypoMg impairs Na/K pump and increases K leakage risk; hyperK blunts Na/K gradient; hyperMg slows conduction and can cause flaccid paralysis; Ca2+–Na+ exchange underlies contractile force and ECG ST changes in ischemia; Mg deficiency worsens ischemic injury. <cite id="81319e7a-0">Magnesium deficiency impairs Na/K pump activity and compromises maintenance of the K gradient, increasing membrane permeability</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium’s roles in energy metabolism, neuromuscular conduction, and NMDA blockade link to muscle contraction and control of neurotransmitter cycling</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-1">Magnesium participates in neural conduction and muscle contraction, controlling excitability and neurotransmitter cycling</cite>.
- Clinical ECG correlates: hyperkalemia shifts the resting potential (peaked T, PR/QT changes), hypokalemia predisposes to U waves and arrhythmias; hypermagnesemia mimics hyperkalemia with PR/QT depression and flaccid paralysis; these effects derive from shared channels/pumps and competitive/blocking actions among K, Na, Mg, and Ca. <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium blocks NMDA receptors and is required for vitamin D activation, linking to calcium channel control and neuromuscular effects</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-1">Magnesium’s regulation of K and Ca-dependent channels underlies effects on neural conduction and muscle function</cite>.

5) Inter-ionic interactions and “other” ions: competition, exchange, and acid–base coupling
- Mg2+ versus Ca2+: “chemical antagonists” at some transporters/channels and “cooperators” in homeostasis. In kidney, CaSR-linked inhibition of NKCC2/ROMK reduces paracellular Ca/Mg shunting; TRPM6 mediates high-affinity Mg reabsorption that competes with Ca2+ in tight junction pathways; Mg also blocks Ca entry through NMDA receptors and supports ATP-dependent Ca extrusion indirectly. <cite id="1215616c-0">High extracellular Ca activates CaSR and inhibits NKCC2 via ROMK effects, suppressing paracellular Ca absorption and linked Mg movement</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">In thick ascending limb, Ca and Mg reabsorb via paracellular pathway; in distal convoluted tubule, TRPM6/TRPM7 and SLC41A1 mediate Mg reabsorption with Na/K ATPase and Na/Mg counter-transport, highlighting competition and coupling with Ca pathways</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is a calcium channel antagonist at NMDA receptors and is essential for ATP-dependent cellular processes including calcium handling</cite>.
- K+ exchange with Na+ and Mg2+: in the distal nephron, ENaC-driven Na entry and Na/K pump extrusion of Na are coupled to K secretion via ROMK/BK; changes in Na delivery and aldosterone shift K/Mg balance. <cite id="1215616c-2">ENaC in distal nephron orchestrates electrogenic Na reabsorption, creating a lumen-negative voltage that drives K secretion via ROMK and BK; regulation of Na delivery by upstream NCC and hormonal sensing in DCT enables adjustments in urinary K and Na</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">DCT K secretion via ROMK/BK and NCC sets context for Mg reabsorption through TRPM6/TRPM7 and SLC41A1, with voltage-gated Cl channels and Na/K ATPase shaping flow</cite>.
- Acid–base and H+ coupling: changes in pH alter protein binding of Ca and Mg, shift intracellular K (H+ for K+ exchange) across RBCs and renal tubules, and can uncouple Na/K pump activity under energy stress; these link acidosis/alkalosis to K, Mg, and Ca derangements. <cite id="81319e7a-0">With magnesium deficiency, energy supply to the Na/K pump falls (ATP-Mg complex), impairing K gradient maintenance and increasing membrane permeability</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">Renal handling of Mg and Ca involves transporter arrays (NKCC2, ROMK, TRPM6, SLC41A1) and CaSR feedback; acid-base perturbations that alter Ca/Mg binding and cellular energetics will propagate to these transporters and gradients</cite>.
- Phosphate and intracellular buffering: intracellular MgATP is the energy currency; phosphate is a product of ATP hydrolysis and a component of Na/K pump stoichiometry (3 Na out, 2 K in per ATP); high phosphate can compete with Mg for some enzyme interactions and influence membrane energetics. <cite id="81319e7a-0">The energy substrate for the Na/K pump is the ATP-Mg2+ complex; hydrolysis provides the transport energy, and Mg deficiency reduces this substrate</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium participates in energy generation (oxidative phosphorylation, glycolysis) and is a cofactor for ATP-dependent enzymes, linking phosphate metabolism to ion transport</cite>.

6) Clinical and therapeutic interactions: how these relationships manifest in patients
- Diuretic effects and electrolyte storms: loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in TAL, decreasing the lumen-positive gradient and paracellular Ca/Mg reabsorption, leading to Ca and Mg loss; thiazides reduce distal Na reabsorption, activating distal K secretion (ROMK/BK) and can cause hypokalemia; potassium-sparing diuretics act downstream (ENaC blockade or aldosterone antagonism) to preserve K; magnesium supplementation is needed when Mg reabsorption is impaired, with risks of hypomagnesemia in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients. <cite id="1215616c-0">In thick ascending limb, NKCC2 and ROMK-driven paracellular reabsorption of Ca and Mg depends on a lumen-positive gradient; activation of CaSR inhibits NKCC2/ROMK and paracellular Ca absorption</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">Loop of Henle NKCC2/ROMK/Na+/K+-ATPase set Ca/Mg reabsorption; in distal convoluted tubule, TRPM6/TRPM7 and SLC41A1 mediate Mg reabsorption with Na/K ATPase and Na/Mg counter-transport</cite> <cite id="1215616c-2">ENaC/ROMK/BK in ASDN mediate electrogenic Na reabsorption and K secretion; shifting from NCC to ENaC dominance increases K loss and Na retention control in response to diet and hormones</cite>.
- Aldosterone excess/deficiency: hyperaldosteronism increases ENaC, Na-K-ATPase, and K excretion with Na retention; adrenal insufficiency reduces Na-K-ATPase, causing hypokalemia and impaired Na/K gradients; in certain disease states (e.g., nephrosis), Na-K-ATPase can be induced without aldosterone, altering Na balance and serum K. <cite id="c5ddf2a5-1">Aldosterone increases apical Na entry and basolateral Na extrusion; latent pumps are recruited by [Na+]i, with aldosterone required for constitution/activation</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-2">In nephrosis, Na-K-ATPase in CCD can increase independent of aldosterone, enabling Na retention despite reduced ENaC; a drop in aldosterone increased serum K in rats</cite>.
- Magnesium deficiency: common with malnutrition, alcoholism, insulin/alkaline stress; impairs Na/K pump (ATP-Mg complex), worsens K loss (hyperkalemia paradoxically can reflect pump failure), increases neuromuscular excitability and ischemic injury; supplementation restores pump function and stabilizes membranes. <cite id="81319e7a-0">Magnesium deficiency reduces ATP-Mg for Na/K pump, impairing K influx into cells and compromising the membrane barrier</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-1">Magnesium is pivotal to regulation of K and Ca via Na+/K+-ATPase and Ca2+-activated K channels, with clinical relevance to sleep and neural function</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is essential for energy production and neuromuscular conduction; deficiency undermines these processes</cite>.
- Magnesium excess: causes GI symptoms, neuromuscular flaccid paralysis, bradycardia/PR depression on ECG by blocking Ca channels and depleting intracellular Ca; treatment is supportive and dialysis in severe cases. <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium blocks NMDA receptors and acts as a calcium channel antagonist, providing mechanistic basis for neuromuscular and cardiac effects of hypermagnesemia</cite>.

7) Putting it together: a dynamic network, not a set of static pairs
- Core energy-and-gradient network: ATP-Mg fuels Na/K pump → K stays intracellular, Na stays extracellular; Na gradient drives Na entry via channels (ENaC) and Na-Ca exchange; K efflux via KCa/ROMK and Na/K pump restores resting potential; Ca2+ entry triggers exocytosis/contraction, limited by Mg block; Ca extrusion uses Na/Ca exchangers and Ca-ATPases with Na/K pump as the global ATP source. <cite id="81319e7a-0">The ATP-Mg complex provides energy for Na/K pump, which maintains K gradients and membrane electrical potential</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-0">Na/K-ATPase subunits and isoforms, regulated by aldosterone and glucocorticoids, underpin tissue-specific gradients</cite> <cite id="1215616c-2">ENaC/ROMK/BK and NCC in distal nephron mirror this coupling in urine composition</cite>.
- Hormonal and receptor cross-talk: aldosterone and glucocorticoids tune Na/K pump and distal Na/K handling; CaSR couples Ca to NKCC2/ROMK and Na/K-ATPase; vitamin D activation depends on Mg, closing a loop between Ca and Mg metabolism. <cite id="c5ddf2a5-0">Aldosterone and glucocorticoids regulate Na/K-ATPase expression via MR and GR</cite> <cite id="1215616c-0">CaSR activation inhibits NKCC2 via ROMK and suppresses paracellular Ca absorption</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is required for conversion of vitamin D to 1,25(OH)2D</cite>.
- “Other” ions as levers and constraints: Cl− cotransports with Na/K/organic solutes (NKCC2, DCT Cl− channels) and shapes K secretion; H+ shifts K and Mg between intra- and extracellular spaces and affects protein binding of Ca/Mg; phosphate is a byproduct of ATP hydrolysis and participates in Na/K stoichiometry and enzyme interactions; bicarbonate buffers H+ to modulate shifts. <cite id="1215616c-1">In distal convoluted tubule, voltage-gated Cl channels and NCC modulate Mg flow, with TRPM6/TRPM7 and SLC41A1 completing reabsorption</cite> <cite id="1215616c-2">Big-K channels (BK) and ROMK mediate flow-dependent K secretion in distal nephron</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-0">Magnesium participates in energy metabolism (ATP), linking phosphate to ion transport energetics</cite>.

Key takeaways: 
- Magnesium is indispensable as an energy cofactor for Na/K pump and as a physiological brake on Ca entry; deficits destabilize K and Ca homeostasis and worsen excitability, while excesses mimic hyperkalemia and depress Ca-mediated function. <cite id="81319e7a-0">Magnesium deficiency reduces ATP-Mg for Na/K pump, impairing K gradient and membrane barrier</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium’s blockade of NMDA receptors stabilizes neuronal excitability</cite>.
- Sodium and potassium are mechanistically linked by a shared pump/channel network with aldosterone-sensitive switches in the distal nephron; their handling directly shapes calcium and magnesium movements via lumen potential, paracellular shunts, and specific transporters. <cite id="c5ddf2a5-1">Aldosterone rapidly links apical Na entry and basolateral Na extrusion in collecting duct</cite> <cite id="1215616c-0">NKCC2/ROMK and claudins drive Ca and Mg paracellular reabsorption in thick ascending limb</cite> <cite id="1215616c-1">DCT TRPM6/SLC41A1 reabsorb Mg with Na/K ATPase and Na/Mg counter-transport</cite>.
- Clinical management should consider cross-talk: correcting Na/K with diuretics affects Mg and Ca; treating hypokalemia must account for Mg repletion; acid–base correction impacts K/Mg/Ca distribution; and parathyroidal/vitamin D–Mg links modulate Ca. <cite id="1215616c-2">Dietary K and low-salt intake shift distal nephron handling (NCC↔ENaC), altering K and Na excretion</cite> <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium is required for vitamin D activation, tying Ca regulation to Mg status</cite>.

Notes on evidence limits and uncertainties:
- Direct, head-to-head quantitative coupling constants among Mg, Na, K, and Ca at the plasma membrane under varying Vm/Pa are derived from model systems and channel biophysics; while mechanistic and clinical correlations are strong, precise numerical cross-effects can vary by cell type and disease. <cite id="81319e7a-2">Magnesium’s voltage-dependent blockade of NMDA receptors and its cofactor roles are well supported</cite> <cite id="c5ddf2a5-0">Na/K-ATPase structure, isoforms, and steroid-regulation are established</cite>.
- Renal transport contributions (TRPM6, SLC41A1, claudins) are supported by targeted reviews and experimental models; absolute contributions per nephron segment differ with diet, age, and hormones and can be context-specific. <cite id="1215616c-1">TRPM6/TRPM7/SLC41A1 mediate Mg reabsorption in DCT with Na/K ATPase and Na/Mg counter-transport</cite> <cite id="1215616c-0">CaSR–NKCC2/ROMK cross-talk modulates paracellular Ca/Mg absorption</cite>.
- Additional human interventional data (e.g., randomized trials quantifying simultaneous Na/K/Mg/Ca changes with diet or drug) and mechanistic studies in different tissues would further refine species- and disease-specific magnitudes.

Title: Regulation of the Human Na/K-ATPase β1 Gene Promoter by Mineralocorticoid and Glucocorticoid Receptors*
Snippet: Na/K-ATPase is an integral membrane protein responsible for the transport of sodium and potassium across the plasma membrane in an ATP-dependent manner (for review, see Refs. 1 and 2). MR is highly homologous to the GR (12,13) which enhances expression of target genes by binding to specific promoter DNA sequences.

Consistently, recent experimental studies demonstrated dissociation between aldosterone levels and Na-K-ATPase activity in CCD. Lourdel et al. (2005) have shown that the presence of aldosterone and activation of epithelial Na + channel in CCD are not required for sodium retention in Puromycin-induced nephrosis (PAN) in rats. These investigators demonstrated increased Na-K-ATPase in CCD in adrenalectomized corticoid-clamped PAN rats. The animals avidly retained Na + despite decreased number and activity of ENaC. This finding was interpreted by the investigators as indicating that induction of Na-K-ATPase was sufficient to increase Na + retention. While the ENaC number and activity were dependent on aldosterone, induction of Na-K-ATPase was aldosterone-independent. 

Thus, our data suggest that in certain circumstances Na-K-ATPase activity in the CCD may change in a fashion independent of alterations in aldosterone levels. Of note, during sodium retention in a model of experimental cirrhosis in rats, Kim et al. (2005) demonstrated downregulation of type 2 11-betahydroxysteroid dehydrogenase in CCD. This allowed increased signaling through mineralocorticoid receptor independent of circulating aldosterone level. Thus, examination of type 2 11-betahydroxysteroid dehydrogenase in CCD may provide some insight into the regulation of Na-K-ATPase in CCD during aging. The fall in aldosterone by 44% raised the risk of hyperkalemia. In fact, concomitant with the fall in aldosterone, the mean serum K + concentration rose from 4.4 to 5.5 mEq/L (20%).

Title: The Mechanisms of Magnesium in Sleep Disorders
Snippet: Magnesium (Mg), the second most abundant mineral in the human body, participates in over 300 biochemical reactions. Serving as an essential cofactor for numerous enzymatic reactions, it plays a pivotal role in maintaining cellular functions and physiological homeostasis. 1 Magnesium is pivotal to a wide array of biological processes, including oxidative phosphorylation, energy generation, glycolysis, and the biosynthesis of proteins and nucleic acids. 2 A large proportion of the body's magnesium is sequestered in bones and cells. The homeostasis of intracellular magnesium ions is intricately intertwined with the metabolism of other intracellular cations, notably potassium (K + ), sodium (Na + ), and calcium (Ca² + ), via mechanisms such as Na + /K + -ATPase, Ca² + -activated K + channels, and other regulatory pathways. This interconnected ion regulation is fundamental to neural conduction within the nervous system, ensuring proper transmission of electrical signals and overall neuronal function. 3 Magnesium ions also participate in muscle contraction, control neuronal excitability, and influence neurotransmitter cycling by regulating the transmembrane transport of other ions. This role is particularly crucial in the regulation of sleep. 4

Snippet: Magnesium is a divalent cation that is obtained from diet, absorbed through intestinal epithelial channels in the gastrointestinal tract, and excreted by the kidney (5). It is an essential electrolyte that is critical for many functions in the human body (6)(7)(8). It is a cofactor for more than 300 biochemical enzymes, such as Na + /K + -ATPase, hexokinase, creatine kinase, protein kinase, and cyclase. It is involved in numerous physiological functions, including energy production, neuromuscular conduction, nucleic acid, and protein synthesis, electrolyte balance, cellular membrane function, glucose metabolism, cardiovascular system regulation, and bone development (5)(6)(7). As a calcium channel antagonist, magnesium blocks the N-methyl-Daspartate (NMDA) receptor in a voltage-dependent manner (5). Magnesium is a cofactor for the ATP-dependent synthesis of glutathione, and thus serves an important role in antioxidant defense (6). Magnesium is also required for the conversion of vitamin D into the active, hormonal form 1,25 (OH) 2 D (6).

Summary
Severe hypomagnesemia can drive hyperkalemia by compromising Na-K-ATPase-dependent K+ homeostasis: reduced Mg2+ availability impairs the activation and energy coupling of the Na-K-ATPase, diminishing K+ influx and eroding the K+ gradient, which together with Na+ overload depolarizes cells and unopposed Na+ entry can elevate extracellular K+ despite impaired renal K+ excretion. Magnesium repletion restores Na-K-ATPase function and shifts K+ back intracellularly, often increasing serum K+ acutely in patients who were low in both Mg and K+ due to inhibited renal K+ excretion. <cite id="b2919055-0">Low magnesium causes impairment of the Mg2+-regulated Na+/K+-ATPase, increasing intracellular sodium and reducing intracellular potassium, creating a less negative resting membrane potential; repletion of Mg2+ increases serum K+ in hypomagnesemic hypokalemic patients, in part by activating ROMK and driving K+ influx into cells</cite>.

Magnesium as an essential cofactor for Na-K-ATPase and cellular consequences
Na-K-ATPase requires Mg2+ both as an activator and as the immediate energy substrate (ATP–Mg2+ complex) for phosphorylation and conformational cycling; Mg deficiency reduces pump activity and the ability to maintain the K+ gradient across the membrane. <cite id="ea52e687-0">The Na+ /K+ pump is activated by magnesium; with magnesium deficiency, impaired pump activity prevents adequate potassium reuptake, and because the energy substrate is the ATP–Mg2+ complex, insufficient Mg2+ diminishes the energy supply and membrane excitability</cite>. <cite id="ea52e687-3">The Na+,K+-ATPase exchanges 3 Na+ for 2 K+ per ATP hydrolyzed via phosphorylation cycles that alternate ion exposure to the intracellular and extracellular sides; passive Na+ influx challenges the pump under physiological conditions</cite>. <cite id="ea52e687-1">Na-K-ATPase activity is a dominant ATP consumer in renal epithelium, and small changes in its activity shift intracellular Na+ and K+ and the driving forces for transepithelial transport of other ions (including Mg and Ca), with the highest activity in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) where the α and β subunits stabilize trafficking and function</cite>. When Mg2+ is limiting, Na-K-ATPase under-phosphorylates and under-cycles, leading to Na+ accumulation and reduced K+ uptake; this depolarizes the cell and weakens the electrochemical K+ gradient. <cite id="b2919055-0">Inhibition of Na+/K+-ATPase in hypomagnesemia increases intracellular sodium and reduces intracellular potassium, producing a less negative resting potential, reflecting the pump’s Mg2+-dependent regulation</cite>.

Summary
Severe hypomagnesemia can drive hyperkalemia by compromising Na-K-ATPase-dependent K+ homeostasis: reduced Mg2+ availability impairs the activation and energy coupling of the Na-K-ATPase, diminishing K+ influx and eroding the K+ gradient, which together with Na+ overload depolarizes cells and unopposed Na+ entry can elevate extracellular K+ despite impaired renal K+ excretion. Magnesium repletion restores Na-K-ATPase function and shifts K+ back intracellularly, often increasing serum K+ acutely in patients who were low in both Mg and K+ due to inhibited renal K+ excretion. <cite id="b2919055-0">Low magnesium causes impairment of the Mg2+-regulated Na+/K+-ATPase, increasing intracellular sodium and reducing intracellular potassium, creating a less negative resting membrane potential; repletion of Mg2+ increases serum K+ in hypomagnesemic hypokalemic patients, in part by activating ROMK and driving K+ influx into cells</cite>.

Magnesium as an essential cofactor for Na-K-ATPase and cellular consequences
Na-K-ATPase requires Mg2+ both as an activator and as the immediate energy substrate (ATP–Mg2+ complex) for phosphorylation and conformational cycling; Mg deficiency reduces pump activity and the ability to maintain the K+ gradient across the membrane. <cite id="ea52e687-0">The Na+ /K+ pump is activated by magnesium; with magnesium deficiency, impaired pump activity prevents adequate potassium reuptake, and because the energy substrate is the ATP–Mg2+ complex, insufficient Mg2+ diminishes the energy supply and membrane excitability</cite>. <cite id="ea52e687-3">The Na+,K+-ATPase exchanges 3 Na+ for 2 K+ per ATP hydrolyzed via phosphorylation cycles that alternate ion exposure to the intracellular and extracellular sides; passive Na+ influx challenges the pump under physiological conditions</cite>. <cite id="ea52e687-1">Na-K-ATPase activity is a dominant ATP consumer in renal epithelium, and small changes in its activity shift intracellular Na+ and K+ and the driving forces for transepithelial transport of other ions (including Mg and Ca), with the highest activity in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) where the α and β subunits stabilize trafficking and function</cite>. When Mg2+ is limiting, Na-K-ATPase under-phosphorylates and under-cycles, leading to Na+ accumulation and reduced K+ uptake; this depolarizes the cell and weakens the electrochemical K+ gradient. <cite id="b2919055-0">Inhibition of Na+/K+-ATPase in hypomagnesemia increases intracellular sodium and reduces intracellular potassium, producing a less negative resting potential, reflecting the pump’s Mg2+-dependent regulation</cite>.

Renal mechanisms: loss of Mg2+ and the renal K+ gradient
Magnesium deficiency also undermines distal nephron K+ handling. <cite id="b2919055-0">Magnesium repletion reduces K+ excretion by activating ROMK; intracellular Mg2+ transiently blocks the ROMK pore, and K+ influx displaces this Mg2+ block to allow entry of the molar amount needed to restore gradient-driven K+ uptake</cite>. In hypomagnesemia, reduced Na-K-ATPase activity in the DCT diminishes the Na+ gradient that drives Mg2+ reabsorption and alters transepithelial driving forces for K+. <cite id="b2919055-4">Changes in intracellular Na+ in DCT alter Na-K-ATPase activity, affecting intracellular K+ and the driving force for Mg transport; Mg reabsorption in the DCT can serve as an in vivo readout of Na-K-ATPase activity</cite>. <cite id="b2919055-2">Renal Mg reabsorption in the DCT depends on apical TRPM6 entry and basolateral Na-K-ATPase activity that creates the Na+ gradient via SLC41A1 exchange; reduced Na-K-ATPase abundance/activity in the DCT explains Mg wasting in genetic and drug-induced hypomagnesemias</cite>. When Na-K-ATPase is impaired, distal K+ delivery and excretion become dysregulated; paradoxically, even as whole-body K+ uptake falls, the reduced gradient and depolarization can facilitate Na+ entry through epithelial pathways (e.g., ENaC) and reduce K+ retention, predisposing to plasma K+ elevation in some settings. <cite id="b2919055-0">Hypomagnesemia-associated hypokalemia reflects reduced cellular K+ uptake and increased renal K+ excretion due to Na+ /K+ -ATPase inhibition, but Mg2+ repletion increases serum K+ by restoring ROMK-mediated K+ influx</cite>.

Although many clinical cases of Mg deficiency present with hypokalemia, severe Mg depletion can contribute to hyperkalemia via two coupled mechanisms: depolarization with impaired K+ gradient and reduced aldosterone-mediated K+ excretion.

1) Cellular depolarization and Na+–K+ imbalance: Severe cytosolic Mg2+ depletion reduces ATP–Mg2+ formation and Na-K-ATPase phosphorylation, impairing K+ influx and widening K+ permeability pathways; the net Na+ influx and reduced K+ gradient depolarize the membrane, opening voltage-gated Na+ channels and facilitating extracellular K+ leakage during diastolic depolarization. <cite id="ea52e687-0">With Mg deficiency, ATP–Mg2+ is insufficient, pump activity falls, and the K+ gradient cannot be maintained, increasing membrane permeability and cellular depolarization</cite>. <cite id="b2919055-0">Low magnesium impairs Mg2+-regulated Na+ /K+ -ATPase, elevating intracellular Na+ and lowering intracellular K+, yielding a less negative resting membrane potential, which supports outward K+ efflux under normal conditions but can paradoxically contribute to membrane depolarization when inward Na+ fluxes are increased</cite>. Severe hypomagnesemia causes hyperkalemia by a two-step process. Clinical implications and therapeutic logic
Clinically, hypomagnesemia should raise suspicion for hyperkalemia when there is profound ECG T-wave tenting, PR prolongation, or pulsual arrhythmias despite low potassium or normal kidneys, because depolarization and Na+ influx can create a false or fluctuating hyperkalemia phenotype. <cite id="b2919055-0">Magnesium deficiency impairs Na+ /K+ -ATPase, alters membrane potential, and is mechanistically linked to arrhythmias; Mg and K+ are tightly coupled, with many hypokalemic cases linked to Mg deficiency</cite>. - Magnesium is essential for Na-K-ATPase activation and energy coupling; deficiency diminishes K+ uptake and promotes Na+ overload and depolarization. <cite id="ea52e687-0">Na-K pump is Mg-activated and uses ATP–Mg2+ as substrate; Mg deficiency reduces pump activity and K+ gradient maintenance</cite>. 
- In the kidney, Na-K-ATPase sets the driving force for DCT Mg and K+ transport; reduced activity in hypomagnesemia alters ROMK function and distal K+ handling. <cite id="b2919055-2">DCT Mg reabsorption depends on Na-K-ATPase–derived Na+ gradient</cite>. <cite id="b2919055-0">Mg2+ binding modulates ROMK; repletion shifts K+ back into cells</cite>.
- Severe hypomagnesemia can produce hyperkalemia via depolarization with impaired K+ gradient and via aldosterone-independent/modified reductions in K+ excretion; correction of Mg often normalizes K+ by restoring pump and epithelial K+ channels. <cite id="b2919055-0">Hypomagnesemia impairs Na+ /K+ -ATPase and can reduce K+ uptake with increased renal excretion (hypokalemia), yet Mg repletion raises serum K+ by restoring Na+ /K+ -ATPase and ROMK</cite>. <cite id="d66b6467-3">Renal defects and altered renin–aldosterone responses can cause persistent hyperkalemia with low urine K+ during Mg infusion</cite>.

Title: Genetic and drug-induced hypomagnesemia: different cause, same mechanism

Mg2+ deficiency is therefore associated with a wide range of clinical effects including muscle cramps, fatigue, seizures and arrhythmias. documents.snippet:
Another aspect of arrhythmogenesis refers to different types of Mg 2+ dependent K + currents playing an essential role against the excessive prolongation of myocardial action potential and having a protecting role against arrhythmia [26]. The mechanisms behind hypomagnesemia-associated hypokalaemia seem to be linked to the alteration of Na-K-ATPase responsible for a decrease in the cellular uptake of K + and increased renal K + excretion due to the inhibition of the Na + /K + -ATPase. Low magnesium causes impairment of the function of Na + /K + -ATPase, which is Mg 2+ regulated and increases intracellular sodium and reduces intracellular potassium levels, creating a less negative resting membrane potential. Magnesium deficiency can also lead to hypokalaemia and hypocalcemia, making the role of establishing the link between pure hypomagnesemia and cardiac arrhythmias somehow difficult. There is a strong relationship between Mg 2+ and K + ; both cations are integral for decreasing cell excitability and stabilizing membrane potentials. Half of the significant hypokalemias seem to be associated with magnesium deficiency; the co-administration of magnesium thus is essential in correcting serum potassium (K + ) concentrations [27]. Enhanced gastrointestinal and renal excretion of K + can also lead to hypokalaemia; however, it was shown that in patients with both hypomagnesemia and hypokalaemia, the repletion of Mg 2+ alone also increased the serum K + level [4,28]. 

The cellular mechanism behind the reduction of K + excretion induced by Mg 2+ repletion is linked to the effect on the ROMK. This inward-rectifying K + current helps flow the potassium ion inside the cells of the apical membrane of the distal tubule. Intracellular magnesium binding to the channel's pore causes a temporary block for efflux of K + . On the other hand, the influx of K + displaces the channel-bent magnesium ion and the maximal needed quantity of K + enters the cell.

documents.title: Genetic and drug-induced hypomagnesemia: different cause, same mechanism
documents.snippet: Magnesium (Mg2+) plays an essential role in many biological processes. Mg2+ deficiency is therefore associated with a wide range of clinical effects including muscle cramps, fatigue, seizures and arrhythmias. To maintain sufficient Mg2+ levels, (re)absorption of Mg2+ in the intestine and kidney is tightly regulated. Genetic defects that disturb Mg2+ uptake pathways, as well as drugs interfering with Mg2+ (re)absorption cause hypomagnesemia. The aim of this review is to provide an overview of the molecular mechanisms underlying genetic and drug-induced Mg2+ deficiencies. This leads to the identification of four main mechanisms that are affected by hypomagnesemia-causing mutations or drugs: luminal transient receptor potential melastatin type 6/7-mediated Mg2+ uptake, paracellular Mg2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop, structural integrity of the distal convoluted tubule and Na+-dependent Mg2+ extrusion driven by the Na+/K+-ATPase. Our analysis demonstrates that genetic and drug-induced causes of hypomagnesemia share common molecular mechanisms. Targeting these shared pathways can lead to novel treatment options for patients with hypomagnesemia.

in DCT is crucial to the final balance of Mg, because changes in Mg reabsorption in PCT and TALH can be compensated for in the DCT, but not more distally in the collecting duct. Mg reabsorption in PCT and TALH is paracellular, while that in DCT is an active transcellular process (de Baaij et al. 2015a). 

Comprehensive reviews of renal Mg handling in health and disease have been published recently (de Baaij et al. 2015a;McCormick and Ellison 2015). We focus here on the role played by the Na,K-ATPase in renal Mg handling, and inherited diseases of Mg balance, with reference primarily to the regulatory FXYD2 subunit. Although the mechanisms of Mg transport in kidneys are quite well understood, the role of the Na,K-ATPase has been less clearly defined. Na,K-ATPase hydrolyses ATP and actively extrudes 3Na ions in exchange for 2K ions per cycle. In the kidney, over 50% of the cellular ATP is utilized by Na,K-ATPase and even small changes in rates of active Na and K transport can have significant effects on cellular Na and K concentrations, and driving forces for transport of other ions such as Mg or Ca. Na,K-ATPase activity varies along the renal tubule and, indeed, the highest Na, K-ATPase activity is found in DCT followed by medullary TALH and PCT (Katz et al. 1979). 

Na,K-ATPase consists of a and b subunits together with a regulatory FXYD subunit in 1:1:1 molecular complex (abFXYD) (Kaplan 2002;Jorgensen et al. 2003). a subunits consist of about 1000 residues with ten transmembrane segments and contain the functional sites for Na, K and ATP binding. b subunits are highly glycosylated single transmembrane segment proteins of about 300 residues, essential for stabilization of the ab complex and normal trafficking and expression in the membrane. There are four isoforms of the a (a1-4) and three isoforms of the b subunit (b1-3) (Blanco and Mercer 1998).

documents.snippet:
Another aspect of arrhythmogenesis refers to different types of Mg 2+ dependent K + currents playing an essential role against the excessive prolongation of myocardial action potential and having a protecting role against arrhythmia [26]. The mechanisms behind hypomagnesemia-associated hypokalaemia seem to be linked to the alteration of Na-K-ATPase responsible for a decrease in the cellular uptake of K + and increased renal K + excretion due to the inhibition of the Na + /K + -ATPase. Low magnesium causes impairment of the function of Na + /K + -ATPase, which is Mg 2+ regulated and increases intracellular sodium and reduces intracellular potassium levels, creating a less negative resting membrane potential. Magnesium deficiency can also lead to hypokalaemia and hypocalcemia, making the role of establishing the link between pure hypomagnesemia and cardiac arrhythmias somehow difficult. There is a strong relationship between Mg 2+ and K + ; both cations are integral for decreasing cell excitability and stabilizing membrane potentials. Half of the significant hypokalemias seem to be associated with magnesium deficiency; the co-administration of magnesium thus is essential in correcting serum potassium (K + ) concentrations [27]. Enhanced gastrointestinal and renal excretion of K + can also lead to hypokalaemia; however, it was shown that in patients with both hypomagnesemia and hypokalaemia, the repletion of Mg 2+ alone also increased the serum K + level [4,28]. 

The cellular mechanism behind the reduction of K + excretion induced by Mg 2+ repletion is linked to the effect on the ROMK. This inward-rectifying K + current helps flow the potassium ion inside the cells of the apical membrane of the distal tubule. Intracellular magnesium binding to the channel's pore causes a temporary block for efflux of K + . On the other hand, the influx of K + displaces the channel-bent magnesium ion and the maximal needed quantity of K + enters the cell.

The Na ϩ ,K ϩ -ATPase (sodium pump) belongs to P-type cation transporting ATPases, which use energy from ATP hydrolysis to establish electrochemical gradients for different ions across cellular membranes. Gastric H ϩ ,K ϩ -ATPase and sarco-plasmic reticulum Ca 2ϩ -ATPase are closely related members (1). The Na ϩ ,K ϩ -ATPase exchanges intracellular Na ϩ for extracellular K ϩ , at a stoichiometry of 3Na ϩ /2K ϩ for each ATP molecule hydrolyzed (2). The functional pump consists of two subunits; ␣ is the catalytic subunit that couples ATP hydrolysis to the uphill transport of ions, and ␤ is a glycoprotein important for targeting and stability of the enzyme complex (3). documents.title: Modulation of the Na,K-pump function by beta subunit isoforms
documents.snippet: To study the role of the Na,K-ATPase beta subunit in the ion transport activity, we have coexpressed the Bufo alpha 1 subunit (alpha 1) with three different isotypes of beta subunits, the Bufo Na,K-ATPase beta 1 (beta 1NaK) or beta 3 (beta 3NaK) subunit or the beta subunit of the rabbit gastric H,K-ATPase (beta HK), by cRNA injection in Xenopus oocyte. We studied the K+ activation kinetics by measuring the Na,K- pump current induced by external K+ under voltage clamp conditions. The endogenous oocyte Na,K-ATPase was selectively inhibited, taking advantage of the large difference in ouabain sensitivity between Xenopus and Bufo Na,K pumps. The K+ half-activation constant (K1/2) was higher in the alpha 1 beta 3NaK than in the alpha 1 beta 1NaK groups in the presence of external Na+, but there was no significant difference in the absence of external Na+. Association of alpha 1 and beta HK subunits produced active Na,K pumps with a much lower apparent affinity for K+ both in the presence and in the absence of external Na+. The voltage dependence of the K1/2 for external K+ was similar with the three beta subunits. Our results indicate that the beta subunit has a significant influence on the ion transport activity of the Na,K pump. The small structural differences between the beta 1NaK and beta 3NaK subunits results in a difference of the apparent affinity for K+ that is measurable only in the presence of external Na+, and thus appears not to be directly related to the K+ binding site. In contrast, association of an alpha 1 subunit with a beta HK subunit results in a Na,K pump in which the K+ binding or translocating mechanisms are altered since the apparent affinity for external K+ is affected even in the absence of external Na+.

Snippet: Hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypokalemia were not found. 

The decreased urinary excretion of calcium and potassium contrasts with the increased urinary excretion found with severe magnesium deficiency in humans, which is indicated by hypocalcemia and hypokalemia. For example, mild or moderate magnesium deficiency might cause increased intracellular calcium by retaining calcium through reduced calcium excretion while assuring that plasma concentrations were not affected. An animal study supports the finding that increased retention and decreased excretion occur in mild or moderate magnesium deficiency. Calcium retention and balance and urinary excretion decreased in old rats fed a moderately magnesium-deficient diet for four weeks [61]. In the case of potassium, decreased urinary excretion of potassium might reflect the body's attempt to retain it for critical biochemical functions that were suppressed by intracellular magnesium deficiency. Thus, the controlled environment metabolic unit findings support the posit that chronic latent magnesium deficiency or mild to moderate magnesium deficiency can cause changes to electrolyte metabolism that contribute to the incidence of cardiovascular disease.

Title: Hypocalcemia and hyperkalemia during magnesium infusion therapy in a pre-eclamptic patient
Snippet: A number of reports in the medical literature describe the association between magnesium and other electrolytes mainly calcium and potassium. While it is well known that hypomagnesemia can cause resistant hypokalemia if not corrected [3], there is little information that explains the relationship between hypermagnesemia and hyperkalemia. In the literature, we found three case reports describing persistent hyperkalemia during magnesium infusion in the setting of preeclampsia treatment [4,5]. Our patient had persistent hyperkalemia despite medical therapy, and the fact that her urine potassium excretion was low (TTKG 4.6) indicates that a renal defect plays a major role in her sustained hyperkalemia. 

The exact mechanism by which magnesium affects renal potassium handling is still unclear. It has been previously postulated that a hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronic state in the setting of hypermagnesemia in preeclamptic patients could be contributory to impaired renal potassium excretion [5]. This is derived from the observation of effects of magnesium infusion on PRA and PAC in two pregnant women with preeclampsia [6]. In this report, PRA was inappropriately low for the pregnant state and PAC was low despite the presence of hyperkalemia. However, as described above, in our patient the renin levels were actually high with normal aldosterone levels, suggesting that an alternative mechanism might explain this relationship. 

Ichihara A. et al. [7] studied the effect of magnesium infusion in normal subjects and similar to our observation, showed that magnesium infusion (postinfusion serum magnesium level 2.32 meq/L) increased renin levels and paradoxically suppressed aldosterone levels. The effect on PRA was mitigated by administration of indomethacin and that on PAC was abolished by administration of diltiazem. The authors thus concluded that the increase in PRA resulted from increased renal prostaglandins and the suppression of PAC was a result of intracellular calcium mobilization [7].
